title: Silverthorne Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Silverthorne wells have a 96 ft median depth, but fractured bedrock can make drilling costs and water supply vary widely.
h1: Silverthorne, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land in Silverthorne means looking past the view and checking the well record. Within five miles, Colorado Division of Water Resources records include 1,259 permitted wells, with 689 recorded as constructed. The available data is uneven: 797 wells report total depth, 263 report pump yield, and 105 report static water level.

Most permits are for domestic or household use, and most wells are identified with an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. That fits the mountain setting around Silverthorne, Dillon, Frisco, and Keystone. A neighboring well is useful evidence, but it is not a guarantee for a new hole on your property.

sections.heading: Silverthorne well depths reflect mountain bedrock
sections.html:
The median recorded well depth near Silverthorne is 96 feet. The middle half runs from 40 to 191 feet, so many wells are relatively shallow, but the spread matters when you request a drilling bid. Half of the reported wells fall outside that middle range. About 51% are under 100 feet, while 40% are between 100 and 300 feet. Another 9% reach 300 to 600 feet, and 1% exceed 600 feet.

The deepest recorded well is 995 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss can produce water through individual fractures rather than a uniform layer, so a nearby shallow completion does not set a reliable limit for your lot. Ask a driller to review nearby logs, access, casing, and grout assumptions before treating the median as a fixed target.

sections.heading: What a Silverthorne well may produce
sections.html:
Reported pump yields are generally workable for household use. The median is 10.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 7.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. The records show 64% producing between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 27% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Another 9% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute.

No reported wells in this dataset are under 1 gallon per minute, but that does not remove the risk of an unsuccessful new hole. A yield test is not the same as storage in the well or guaranteed flow during every season. Confirm the permit's allowed use, storage needs, and any household demand before relying on a production number. An exempt household-use well still has Colorado limits, including the 35 gallons-per-minute pumping limit.

sections.heading: Water levels around Silverthorne
sections.html:
Among the wells reporting static water level, the median depth to water is 22 feet. The middle half measures from 12 to 60 feet below the surface. That is useful for estimating pump setting and construction, but static water level is not the same as the level while pumping. It can also vary with location, season, recharge, and nearby pumping.

The decade figures do not show a simple dropping water table. The median measured depth to water was 70 feet in the 1990s, 50 feet in the 2010s, and 14 feet in the 2020s. Those measurements come from different wells and locations, so the change should not be read as a basin-wide trend. Have the driller measure the actual well and review the original log before sizing equipment.

sections.heading: Permit history and drillers in the local record
sections.html:
Permit activity near Silverthorne spans decades. Records show 9 permits from the 1950s, 94 from the 1960s, 119 from the 1970s, 155 from the 1980s, and 258 from the 1990s. There were 209 in the 2000s, 77 in the 2010s, and 118 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most active names in these records are Buena Vista Drilling (Shelton, William L) with 163 wells, Authorized (Pe, Pg) with 155, and Golden Eagle Drilling Corporation (Shelton, Joe Wayne) with 104. Treat this as permit history, not a recommendation. Verify current licensing, availability, insurance, and experience with your access conditions.

sections.heading: What drilling costs near Silverthorne
sections.html:
Silverthorne drilling commonly means working through fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. The cost model uses a drilling rate of $65 to $100 per foot. At the local median depth of 96 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $6,200 to $9,600.

That is not the complete water-system price. A finished well including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $12,200 to $21,600 at the median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, casing or grout requirements, hard rock, and power distance can move the bid higher. Request a written estimate that separates drilling, casing, grout, development, pump equipment, trenching, electrical, testing, and permits so competing bids describe the same work.

sections.heading: Risks to investigate before closing or building
sections.html:
Low yield and dry-hole risk remain important in fractured bedrock, even though reported nearby yields are mostly moderate or strong. Confirm the well construction report, pump test, static water level, water-quality results, and legal use before buying. The permit use mix is 60% domestic or household, 24% monitoring, 3% stock, and 1% irrigation, so a monitoring well is not evidence of a usable household supply.

Environmental review also matters. Within about ten miles, the mapped record includes 12 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 37 historic mine features, and 7 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These findings do not automatically mean your water is unsafe, but they justify testing and checking site history. Confirm septic setbacks, drainfield space, winter access, building location, and local water-right requirements before finalizing a lot plan.

sections.heading: A practical plan for a Silverthorne lot
sections.html:
Start with the DWR permit and construction records for the property and nearby wells in Silverthorne, Dillon, Frisco, and Keystone. Compare depths, reported yields, aquifer descriptions, static levels, and the dates of measurements. Then have a licensed driller inspect the proposed access route and identify where a rig, casing materials, pump equipment, and spoils can be handled.

For a new build, coordinate the well location with the septic system, foundation, driveway, utility trench, and winter snow storage before drilling. Confirm the intended household use is allowed by the permit and that an augmentation plan is not required for the property or basin. Budget for the complete installed system rather than the drilling footage alone. Finally, make water-quality testing, well-flow testing, and a review of construction records conditions of the purchase when the property depends on private water.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Silverthorne?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Silverthorne is 96 feet. The middle half runs from 40 to 191 feet, and the deepest record reaches 995 feet. About 51% are under 100 feet, but fractured granite and gneiss can make a new well much deeper than a nearby completion.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Silverthorne?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 96-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $6,200 to $9,600. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $12,200 to $21,600. Difficult access or deeper drilling can increase the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Silverthorne wells produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a 10.0-gallon-per-minute median, with the middle half from 7.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. About 64% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute and 27% report more than 15. Yield records are available for 263 wells, so confirm the actual property’s test.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Silverthorne?
faq.a: Safety depends on the individual well and its surroundings, not just the town. The mapped area includes 12 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 37 historic mine features, and 7 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the well for relevant contaminants, review site history, and inspect the casing, grout, and sanitary seal.

faq.q: Is Silverthorne well water running out?
faq.a: The available static-level series does not show a simple dropping trend. Median depth to water was 70 feet in the 1990s, 50 feet in the 2010s, and 14 feet in the 2020s. Those figures come from different wells, so they cannot predict one property. Obtain a current measurement and pumping test.
